why: Valid substrings live inside maximal vowel-only blocks and must contain all five vowels. For each right end, a window that shrinks its left side to the tightest start still holding all five tells you how many starts work.
hints: A consonant can never be in a valid substring, so split the string into blocks of vowels only.
Inside a block, for each right end r find the largest left l such that s[l..r] still contains all five vowels; every start from the block's beginning up to l works.
Sliding window with vowel counts: add s[r], move l right while s[l] occurs more than once, and when all five are present add (l - blockStart + 1). O(n).
pitfalls: Reset counts at every consonant; windows may not cross one.
Count substrings by position: equal strings at different positions are counted separately.
The answer can be about n^2 / 2; fine in Python, use long elsewhere.
